newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - German measures threaten convergence.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - German measures threaten convergence.

text.p: Germany may be able to plug the hole in its deficit to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) but relying on one-off cash-raising measures puts EMU and further bond convergence at risk, analysts said on Friday.
"The main message that we can extract from all of this is for international investors to sell European bonds," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London.
"It's the best way now to avoid all the questions. Are we going to have a soft EMU? Is EMU going to go ahead at all?" Reed said. "You're just not being paid for all the risks."

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, faced with a 18 billion mark shortfall in tax revenues this year on top of previous forecasts, has said the government was planning on speedier privatisation and a spending freeze.
Waigel also contemplated tax rises and a revaluation of the Bundesbank gold reserves to raise extra revenue on paper.

Yields of peripheral European bond markets have already sharply converged against German Bund yields since the start of 1996 on the belief EMU would go forward as planned in 1999 with a wide group of participants.
The 10-year BTP/Bund yield spread, for example, has narrowed to around 150 basis points from around 475 at the beginning of 1996.
But Huw Roberts, European bonds strategist at NatWest Capital Markets in London, said Germany's revenue-raising plans would make investors disillusioned with EMU altogether.
He said monetary policy would have to take up the slack to stimulate growth, which would keep the mark and therefore Bunds weak.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see the spread between the U.S. and Germany perhaps come in a little bit," Roberts said.
Yields of Italy and Spain could ease slightly further towards Bund yields, but the spreads were already very tight.
Roberts expected the T-note/Bund spread to narrow aggressively in the medium-term after a possible U.S. rate hike which, in the nearer term is seen as bearish for Treasuries.

Some analysts however said that if Germany were allowed to fudge the criteria other countries like Italy and Spain could too, bolstering their EMU chances and extending bond convergenge against Bunds.

"The more difficult this (EMU) will be for Germany to make it, the more they are likely to soften the criteria slightly for everybody else," said Bronwyn Curtis, chief economist at Nomura International in London.
"If you think that Spain is going to be in, the spread should be something like 40 over Bunds," she said. The 10-year Bonos/Bund yield spread is currently 80 basis points.
Reed at BZW would however said for investors who did want to be exposed to Europe, such as Japanese-based bond buyers looking to pick up yield, British gilts would be the best bet.
The gilt/Bund spread was at 140 basis points at 1315 GMT.
"We think that spread will come down further, towards 100," Reed said.
